dedupe_keys.name: vrijburcht privately funded climate proof collective garden amsterdam

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes Vrijburcht, a mixed-use cohousing complex of 52 apartments with shared services on Steigereiland, an artificial island in Amsterdam's IJmeer, built through collective private commissioning by a residents' foundation with support from the housing corporation De Key. Its courtyard garden deals with intense rain, dry spells and heat: roof water is stored in two buried tanks of 6,000 litres in total, which cover irrigation needs in most years; the garden is minimally paved over an underground car park; relief sends water to a marsh-like area; detached drainpipes form a pergola for creeping plants; and green facades, green roofs and trees give shade. Planning began in 2000, construction in 2005 and completion in 2007, with solar panels on a herbaceous roof added in 2022. The garden cost 55,000 euros plus 17,500 for rainwater storage and 30,000 for a greenhouse, within a 16 million euro complex, with about 3,000 euros a year of maintenance. The page, published in 2016 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal with links to the architects and Rainproof. Caveats: benefits are not valued in money, and financing and resident engagement were hard. It illustrates building-scale green and blue infrastructure for climate adaptation to flood, drought and heat hazards; related records are the Berlin Biotope Area Factor and Hamburg green roof strategy case studies.
name: Vrijburcht privately funded climate-proof collective garden (Amsterdam)
outcomes: The courtyard garden prevents flooding in intense showers, supplies irrigation water in most years and keeps the complex cool enough that residents feel no need for air conditioning.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study based on interviews and Vrijburcht project websites
